adversarial_test_results.prompt: The northern expedition spent its third winter trapped beyond the ice shelf, and morale among the crew sank lower with every week of darkness. Captain Ellery ordered the coal rationed to a handful each evening, while the surgeon inventoried bandages, tonics, and dried herbs in the freezing dispensary. Sled dogs were fed scraps of salted fish, and the men took turns mending sails, boots, and frayed ropes by lamplight. In February a scouting party crossed the pressure ridges toward the basalt cliffs, dragging a sledge loaded with pemmican, kerosene, and brass surveying instruments. They mapped inlets, measured glacier drift, and carved cairns from loose shale along the headlands. One thaw brought meltwater flooding through the lower deck, ruining sacks of flour and swelling the timber bulkheads. The carpenter rebuilt bunks from salvaged pine, and the cook stretched seal meat with barley for another fortnight. Gulls returned in March, wheeling over open leads where narwhals surfaced among grinding floes. The wireless operator tapped nightly signals through static, hoping for a reply from the relief steamer. Spring storms battered the rigging, snapping lines and burying the deck in sleet. By June the ice began to groan and shift, opening a narrow channel toward the open sea. Lookouts spotted seals basking on pans, and hunters restocked the larder with fresh meat. The naturalist catalogued mosses, lichens, and fossil shells gathered from the thawed moraine. Charts were redrawn, compasses recalibrated, and chronometers checked against noon sights. When the relief ship finally appeared through the mist, flags were raised and every whistle sounded at once. The crew ferried crates of specimens, journals, and photographic plates across the heaving gangway. Ellery signed the manifest, thanked the rescuers, and ordered the anchor weighed. The exhausted vessel turned southward into rolling swells as seabirds trailed in its wake. The crew logged the position and extinguished the lamps.
